clinicalPearls: A rare pulmonary infection caused by the dimorphic soil fungi of the Emmonsia genus (notably Emmonsia crescens), which chiefly infect burrowing rodents
Humans acquire it by inhaling conidia from soil, an exposure linked to rural, agricultural, and excavation activities
The inhaled conidia do not replicate in the lung but enlarge enormously into thick-walled structures called adiaspores, which provoke a granulomatous reaction
Because the fungus does not multiply, disease severity depends on the number of spores inhaled: a small inoculum may be asymptomatic while a heavy exposure can cause diffuse illness
Clinical presentation ranges from an incidental pulmonary nodule to fever, cough, dyspnoea, and a diffuse reticulonodular or miliary pattern in heavy exposures
Diagnosis is histological, showing the characteristic large adiaspores with thick walls surrounded by granulomas, usually on lung biopsy
Localised disease is often self-limiting; extensive or symptomatic disease is treated with antifungal agents, sometimes with corticosteroids to dampen the granulomatous response
reference.pathophysiology: Emmonsia species are dimorphic fungi that live in soil and infect the lungs of small burrowing mammals. When a person inhales the airborne conidia, body temperature triggers conversion not into replicating yeast but into a unique enlarging spore, the adiaspore, which swells to a large thick-walled sphere without dividing or budding. The lack of replication means the organism cannot disseminate in the usual sense, and the burden of disease is set by the size of the inhaled inoculum. Each adiaspore acts as a persistent antigenic focus that stimulates a granulomatous inflammatory reaction in the surrounding lung. With a light exposure only scattered granulomas form, whereas a massive inhalation produces widespread granulomatous pneumonitis and impaired gas exchange. Note that some organisms formerly grouped with Emmonsia (such as Emergomyces) instead cause true disseminated dimorphic infection in the immunocompromised and are distinct from classical adiaspiromycosis.
additionalDifferentials: Pulmonary tuberculosis and other mycobacterial disease
Histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, and other endemic mycoses
Miliary or metastatic pulmonary nodular disease
Emergomycosis (disseminated dimorphic fungal infection in the immunocompromised)
additionalInvestigations: Lung biopsy with histopathology demonstrating large thick-walled adiaspores within granulomas
Chest imaging (radiograph and CT) to characterise nodular, reticulonodular, or miliary patterns
Fungal culture and molecular identification of Emmonsia species
Exposure history focusing on soil, rural, and excavation activities
Investigations to exclude tuberculosis and endemic mycoses
Assessment of immune status to distinguish classical adiaspiromycosis from disseminated dimorphic infection
redFlags: Diffuse bilateral pulmonary involvement with hypoxaemia after heavy spore exposure
Disseminated disease suggesting an alternative dimorphic fungus in an immunocompromised host
Failure to improve, prompting reconsideration of tuberculosis or malignancy
reference.prognosis: Localised, low-inoculum disease is frequently self-limiting with an excellent outlook, whereas heavy-exposure diffuse pulmonary disease can cause significant respiratory compromise but usually responds to antifungal therapy and supportive care.
pitfalls: Mistaking pulmonary nodules for tuberculosis or malignancy and missing the histological adiaspores
Assuming the organism disseminates like other dimorphic fungi, when classical adiaspiromycosis does not replicate in tissue
Confusing adiaspiromycosis with disseminated emergomycosis in immunocompromised patients
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
UpToDate: Adiaspiromycosis and infections due to Emmonsia species
management: Treat symptomatic or diffuse pulmonary disease with systemic antifungal therapy such as an azole (itraconazole) or amphotericin B for severe illness
Observe asymptomatic low-inoculum disease, such as an incidental solitary granuloma, without antifungal treatment
Provide supportive respiratory care including supplemental oxygen and ventilatory support in heavy-exposure granulomatous pneumonitis
Consider adjunctive corticosteroids to attenuate the granulomatous inflammatory response in severe diffuse disease
Monitor with serial chest imaging and respiratory function to track resolution or progression
Advise avoidance of further heavy soil and dust exposure through appropriate respiratory protection
Refer to infectious diseases and respiratory specialists and exclude tuberculosis and endemic mycoses
